Where it began

Gordon Greenidge was born in Saint Peter, Barbados, on 1 May 1951. His grandmother looked after him for some years while his mother worked in England, and at 14 he joined her in Reading. His school side there won the local schools league, and in 1967 a score of 135 for the Berkshire Bantams against Wiltshire brought offers of a trial from Hampshire and Warwickshire.

He chose Hampshire, arriving in 1968 at 17. Young players had other jobs too, and his included painting the seats around the ground. A big summer for the second eleven in 1970 earned him a first-team place, opening alongside Barry Richards, a partnership he looked back on as both a schooling and an inspiration.

The player

He could have played for England but chose the West Indies, and he made 93 and 107 in his first Test, against India at Bangalore in 1974. In all he played 108 Tests from 1974 to 1991, scoring 7,558 runs at 44.72 with 19 hundreds and 34 fifties, and holding 96 catches.

The summer of 1984 brought his most famous day. Set 342 to win at Lord's on the final afternoon, the West Indies were expected to play for a draw. Greenidge had other plans, made 214 not out and won the match. He followed it with 223 at Old Trafford. His last double hundred, 226 against Australia in Barbados in 1991, was also his highest Test score.

What made him special

Strength through the shoulders and arms let him hit the ball very hard indeed, yet he was also a fine player of the moving ball and a superb slip fielder. With Desmond Haynes he formed one of the great opening pairs: together they put on 6,482 runs in Tests, with 16 century stands for the first wicket. Haynes, generous to a fault, reckoned Gordon the better player, especially against spin.

He was a reserved man who took a lean spell hard. After a difficult tour of Australia in 1975–76 he resolved to become impossible to leave out, and he did, scoring more than a thousand runs on the 1976 tour of England. Wisden named him a Cricketer of the Year in 1977.

Away from the middle

After playing he turned to coaching, and his time with Bangladesh changed that country's cricket. Under him they won the 1997 ICC Trophy, which carried them to their first World Cup in 1999 and on towards Test status. Bangladesh made him an honorary citizen. He later sat on the West Indies selection panel alongside Sir Viv Richards.

He was made an MBE in 1985, entered the ICC Cricket Hall of Fame among its first inductees in 2009 and was knighted in 2020 for services to cricket and the development of sport. A primary school in Barbados carries his name.

And finally

In 1990, in his 100th Test, he and Haynes opened against England in Antigua and put on 298 before either was out. Greenidge made 149 and was run out, which is about the only way bowlers seemed able to stop him that day.
